newsitem.title: USA: Barshefsky encouraged by EU letter on technology.
newsitem.headline: Barshefsky encouraged by EU letter on technology.

text.p: Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Thursday she was encouraged by a letter from the European Union this week on efforts to move forward on a global information technology agreement, but Europe lacked unity on the issue.

"I am encouraged, but I don't think we're there yet," Barshefsky told reporters following a speech to a business group. She said she will discuss the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) late Thursday with European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

"He and I will have a frank discussion," Barshefsky said. "Clearly Europe has to come to a rapid decision on this issue. We will not be able to move forward on this initiative ... without Europe because we will not let Europe free-ride on our tariff reductions."
Brittan and Barshefsky are in Seattle for a quadrilateral trade ministers meeting Friday and Saturday that will also include Canada's Arthur Eggleton and Japan's Shunpei Tsukahara.

Barshefsky declined to discuss the content of the letter, but EU sources in Brussels said that Europe was backing down from an ultimatum insisting on European inclusion in a U.S.- Japan semiconductor alliance in order to press for a wider ITA agreement.
The letter was said to suggest that work on the ITA could begin if the "discriminatory aspects" of the U.S.-Japan chip alliance were not applied until after the ITA were finalized.

But Barshefsky said the semiconductor issue can be easily resolved and Europe appears to be backing away from the ITA because it does not have full agreement among its members. Brittan has denied that Europe is backing away from the ITA.

The ITA would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of information technologies, including computer chips and telephone equipment. U.S. trade and industry officials have said that some EU member states are seeking other trade concessions as a price for ending duties on information technology.

"There is no question that Europe is holding back on the ITA, using as an excuse the issue of semiconductors, which we think is readily resolveable, or using as an excuse the need to link ITA with other unrelated issues," Barshefsky said.
"It is clear there is, at this point, no unanimity among the (EU) member states to move forward as aggressively as we, Canada, Japan and others are ready to move," she added.
